title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes Fragment 96 (N. Fuss) of the Opera postuma. In it Euler gives what he calls a much simpler proof of his earlier rule for πa, the number of integers ≤ a that are prime to a. In modern notation πa = φ(a), with the convention π1 = 1.

The tool is a lemma from the previous page. If a > 1 and gcd(q,a) = 1, then any a consecutive terms p, p+q, …, p+(a−1)q run through every residue class mod a. Euler states it for every a; for a = 1 it is trivial.

(1) The array. List the totatives 1 = t₁ < α < β < … < a−1 of a, and form the n×φ(a) array of numbers ka + t (k = 0…n−1). Row k holds exactly the integers in (ka, (k+1)a) that are prime to a, because gcd(ka+t, a) = gcd(t, a). So the whole array is the set of integers in [1, na] prime to a, and there are nφ(a) of them. Each column is an arithmetic progression with difference a.

(2) Prime powers. Take n = a^{m−1}. An integer is prime to a^m exactly when it is prime to a. Hence φ(a^m) = a^{m−1}φ(a) for every a, not only primes. For a prime p this gives φ(p^m) = p^{m−1}(p−1).

(3) Multiplicativity. Let gcd(a,b) = 1 and take n = b. Each column t, a+t, …, (b−1)a+t has b terms with difference a, and a is prime to b. By the lemma the column is a complete residue system mod b, so it contains exactly φ(b) terms prime to b. There are φ(a) columns. Hence the count of numbers ≤ ab prime to both a and b, that is prime to ab, is φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b). This is a combinatorial form of the Chinese-remainder argument.

(4) Consequences. Euler gives a table of φ(1) to φ(16). Extending by induction to pairwise coprime factors gives φ(a^α b^β c^γ d^δ) = a^{α−1}φ(a)·b^{β−1}φ(b)·c^{γ−1}φ(c)·d^{δ−1}φ(d), with a, b, c, d pairwise coprime. For primes this is the usual product formula. The source is cited as A. m. T. III p. 182–184.
errors: Table entry π16 = 7 is wrong: φ(16) = 8 (the odd numbers 1, 3, …, 15). It contradicts Euler's own corollary, which gives 2³·(2−1) = 8. The image shows 7, so this is a printing or copying error, not a transcription one.
In the array, the second row ends 'a+γ … a−1' as printed; it should be '2a−1'.

Minor imprecisions in wording. 'Ab 0 usque ad a' should read 1 ≤ x ≤ a. The convention π1 = 1 (counting 1 as prime to itself) is needed for the formulas to hold when a or b equals 1. The last formula needs a, b, c, d pairwise coprime, which Euler does assume ('inter se primi').

The lemma is stated as giving all residues; the solution silently uses the fact that a complete residue system mod b contains exactly φ(b) elements prime to b. This is correct but unstated. The extension to four factors 'hinc porro patet' is an implicit induction.

ideas.what: Euler's π-notation for the number of integers ≤ a that are prime to a
ideas.modern_name: Euler's totient function φ(n) (symbol φ due to Gauss)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1763, E271), notation φ from Gauss (1801)
ideas.where_published: E271 'Theoremata arithmetica nova methodo demonstrata' (Novi Comm. Petrop. 8, 1763); also later papers such as E564

ideas.what: φ(a^m) = a^{m−1}φ(a) for arbitrary a, proved by partitioning [1, a^m] into blocks of length a
ideas.modern_name: Totient of a power: φ(n^k) = n^{k−1}φ(n)
ideas.where_published: E271 (prime-power case and rule); the general-a form here is a slight variant

ideas.what: Proof of φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for coprime a, b using an n×φ(a) array. Columns are progressions with difference a, hence complete residue systems mod b.
ideas.modern_name: Multiplicativity of φ via the rectangular-array / Chinese-remainder counting proof
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E271) for the result; this array proof is the standard textbook proof, usually unattributed (Gauss, Disquisitiones art. 38, gives another proof)
ideas.where_published: The result is in E271; whether this exact array proof appears in Euler's published papers is unsure. It is published posthumously here (Opera postuma 1862, Fragment 96).

ideas.what: Product formula for φ(N) from the prime factorisation of N

missed.claim: The now-standard textbook 'array' proof of the multiplicativity of φ appears in Euler's notebooks, which Euler himself calls a much simpler demonstration than his published one. If his published proof in E271 differs, this fragment is a (minor) early source for the textbook proof, which is usually given without attribution. This is a historiographical attribution point only, not new mathematics.
missed.quote: jam consideretur prima series verticalis, quae est 1, a+1, 2a+1, … (b−1)a+1, quae quia est arithmetica, ejusque differentia a est prima ad b, numerus terminorum ad b primorum = πb
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only for the history of elementary number-theory pedagogy: it shows that the standard proof goes back to Euler's own notebooks.

deep.surprise_reason: All the results (the totient, φ(p^m), multiplicativity, the product formula) are well known and credited to Euler from E271. The only mildly interesting point is that the clean array proof, now the textbook standard, is in his notebook. It is already published (1862) and mathematically routine. There is also an arithmetic slip in the table (π16 = 7).
transcription_corrections: Row 2 of the array ends '… a−1' in both the print and the transcription; the intended value is 2a−1 (a printing error, faithfully transcribed).
The table entry 'π16 = 7' matches the image; it is a printing error for 8, not a transcription error.
In the image the solution to the first problem reads 'cui ergo aequalis πaa' — the transcription is correct. The multiplications 'a.πa' and 'πa.πb' are products.
